**Sharing helps when tasks need similar features and hurts when their updates conflict.** Click prediction may favor attention-grabbing content, while satisfaction prediction may penalize that same content. If both tasks must use exactly the same representation, improving one can damage the other: negative transfer. [1](https://research.google/pubs/modeling-task-relationships-in-multi-task-learning-with-multi-gate-mixture-of-experts/)

A simple gradient picture helps. If task A wants a shared parameter to increase and task B wants it to decrease, their updates can cancel or one can dominate. Differences in label frequency and loss scale can make the larger task win even when the smaller task is more important.

**MMoE gives tasks different mixtures of shared experts.** Each task has its own gate, so click and satisfaction models can emphasize different expert outputs. PLE makes shared and task-specific paths more explicit across layers, reducing compulsory sharing where tasks diverge. Neither architecture guarantees compatibility or fixes biased labels automatically.

Compare each task against a separate-model baseline, and inspect missing labels and gradient/loss scales. A weighted average can hide unacceptable deterioration in a priority task. Use explicit constraints or a Pareto comparison to decide the tradeoff. Architecture is one control; better label definitions, task weighting, and training populations may matter just as much.

**Technical details and references.**

Negative transfer occurs when shared parameters receive conflicting task gradients or must represent incompatible patterns. Improving click prediction can harm conversion or satisfaction, especially when labels and populations differ. [1](https://research.google/pubs/modeling-task-relationships-in-multi-task-learning-with-multi-gate-mixture-of-experts/)

MMoE uses shared experts with task-specific gates, allowing each task a different mixture. PLE separates shared and task-specific experts across layers, restricting which information is passed where. These designs reduce forced sharing but do not guarantee positive transfer or solve label bias.

Measure per-task gradient alignment, data availability, loss scales, and performance against separate-model baselines. Tune task weighting and missing-label handling. A single weighted average metric can hide a harmed high-priority task; use explicit constraints or a Pareto analysis before selecting the final model.
